Computer Organization and Architecture (CSE23CT201) · Sri Ramachandra Faculty of Engineering and Technology
A companion to the main Unit 4 notes. It carries only the Unit-4 topics that M. Morris Mano (Chapter 12) develops but Hamacher, Vranesic & Zaky (Chapter 8) has no dedicated treatment of. Same figures, wording and worked examples as the full notes.
How to use this supplement. Topics that both textbooks cover — Memory Hierarchy, Main Memory (RAM/ROM chips), Auxiliary Memory, Cache Memory, and the core of Virtual Memory (paging, page tables, page faults) — are intentionally left out here; study those from the Hamacher-based main notes. What remains below is the Mano-only material: Associative Memory (Hamacher has no such section), Mano’s associative-memory page table (the one novel piece inside his virtual-memory section), and Memory Management Hardware (segmentation, segmented-page mapping and the segment descriptor — Hamacher only mentions the MMU/TLB in passing).

1. Associative Memory

Mano §12-4  (Hamacher has no dedicated section on this — it only uses associative searching inside its cache mapping, which is why this topic is taught from Mano alone)

1.1 Why search by content instead of by address?

  • Many data-processing applications require searching a table for an item, rather than reading a known address. The established way is to store the table sequentially and search it address by address — the number of accesses needed depends on the search algorithm and can be large.
  • Search time can be reduced considerably if stored data can be identified for access by the content of the data itself, rather than by its address. A memory unit accessed this way is called an associative memory or content-addressable memory (CAM).
  • An associative memory is accessed simultaneously and in parallel on the basis of data content. When a word is written, no address is given; the memory finds an empty unused location by itself. To read, the content of the word, or part of it, is specified, and the memory locates all words that match and marks them for reading.
  • Because every word is compared in parallel, associative memory is more expensive than ordinary RAM (each cell needs its own comparison logic as well as storage), so it is reserved for applications where search time is critical and must be very short.

1.2 Hardware organization

  • An associative memory consists of a memory array (holding m words of n bits each), plus two special registers: the argument register (A), holding the word being searched for, and the key register (K), which masks which bits of the argument actually take part in the comparison.
  • Every word in the array is compared, bit by bit and in parallel, against the argument register — but only in bit positions where the corresponding key-register bit is 1. If the key register is all 1s, the entire argument word is compared against every memory word.
  • The match register (M) has one bit per memory word; after the comparison, Mi is set to 1 for every word i whose unmasked bits all match the argument — those words are then read out.
Figure 12-6 — Block diagram of associative memory (Mano, p.457): the Argument register (A) and Key register (K) feed the associative memory array and logic, which sets bits in the Match register (M) for every matching word.

1.3 Worked example — masked comparison

WORKED EXAMPLE (from Mano)

Suppose only the three left-most bits of A and K matter (K has 1s only in those positions):

A = 101 111100 K = 111 000000 Word 1 = 100 111100 → no match (first 3 bits differ: 101 vs 100) Word 2 = 101 000001 → match (first 3 bits agree: 101 = 101; remaining bits are masked out by K and ignored)

Word 2 matches the unmasked argument field even though its last six bits look nothing like the argument’s — because K = 0 in those positions, they simply aren’t compared.

1.4 The cell array and match logic

  • Each cell in the array is written Cij — word i, bit j. A bit Aj of the argument is compared with every column j across all words, but only where Kj = 1.
Figure 12-7 — Associative memory of m words, n cells per word (Mano, p.458). Each column j receives argument bit A_j and key bit K_j; each cell C_ij feeds its word’s match bit M_i.
  • The match logic for one word compares, bit by bit, the stored bit Fij against the argument bit Aj, but the key bit Kj can force a position to be treated as an automatic match: the comparison term is xj + Kj′, so when Kj = 0 the term is forced to 1 (always “equal”) regardless of the actual bit values.
  • The full match equation for word i is the AND of every bit position’s term: Mi = Πj=1..n (AjFij + Aj′Fij′ + Kj′) — every unmasked bit must agree for Mi to become 1.
Figure 12-8 — One cell of associative memory (Mano, p.459). A flip-flop F_ij stores the bit; read/write/match logic compares the stored value against A_j and K_j to help set M_i.
Figure 12-9 — Match logic for one word of associative memory (Mano, p.461). Each column contributes an AND/OR/inverter term; all n terms feed a common AND gate producing that word’s match bit M_i.

1.5 Reading, writing, and tag bits

  • Read: if more than one word matches, the matched words are read out one at a time by scanning the match register. If the memory excludes an all-zero word from being a valid entry, an all-zero output on the read lines itself signals “not found.”
  • Write: entries can be loaded in sequence like ordinary random-access memory (decoding d address lines to select 1-of-2d words), making the device a normal RAM for writing and a CAM only for reading.
  • Where words are added and deleted at different times, a tag register (one bit per word) distinguishes active from inactive entries — a word is deleted simply by clearing its tag bit, and a new word is stored in the first location whose tag bit reads 0.

CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING

  1. Define associative memory / content-addressable memory, and explain how it differs from ordinary random-access memory. [4M]
  2. What are the argument register and key register used for, and what happens when the key register is all zeros? [6M]
  3. Draw the block diagram of associative memory and label the match register. [6M]
  4. Obtain the match logic function Mi for one word of associative memory, including the effect of the key bits. [6M]
  5. What additional logic is needed to give a no-match result for a word in associative memory when all its key bits are zero? [4M]
  6. Explain how a tag register supports writing into an associative memory whose entries are added and deleted at different times. [4M]

2. The Associative Memory Page Table

Mano §12-6 — the one part of Mano’s virtual-memory section with no counterpart in Hamacher. (Paging, page faults and the ordinary page table are taught from Hamacher in the main notes; this is the associative-memory variant Mano adds, and it is the bridge from Chapter 1 to the TLB in Chapter 3.)

2.1 Associative memory as a fast page table

  • A conventional random-access page table is inefficient: it needs one entry for every page even though, at any time, only a handful of pages are actually resident (blocks are far fewer than pages). Most of the table sits empty.
  • A more efficient scheme stores the page table itself as an associative memory, with only as many entries as there are blocks in main memory: each word holds a page number together with its block number. The virtual page number is presented as the search argument; a match returns the block number directly — no match means a page fault.
Figure 12-20 — An associative memory page table (Mano, p.474): the argument register holds the page number; each associative-memory word stores a (page number, block number) pair, sized to the number of blocks rather than the number of pages.

3. Memory Management Hardware

Mano §12-7 · Hamacher’s brief MMU/TLB references

3.1 What a memory management unit does

  • In a multiprogramming environment, many programs reside in memory simultaneously, and the amount of memory in use by any one program needs to change as it runs. A memory management unit (MMU) is the collection of hardware and software procedures that manages this.
  • Its basic components: (1) a facility for dynamic storage relocation that maps logical (program-generated) addresses into physical memory addresses; (2) provision for sharing common programs among different users without keeping multiple copies in memory; (3) protection of information against unauthorized access, and prevention of one user’s program from changing another’s.
  • The address generated by a segmented program is called a logical address. It is similar to a virtual address, except that logical address space is organized into variable-length segments rather than uniform, fixed-length pages.

3.2 Segments, and segmented-page mapping

  • A segment is a set of logically related instructions or data given a name — e.g. a subroutine, an array, a table, or a whole user program. Segments let several users share a single copy of a common program (such as a compiler) while each keeps a private copy of their own data.
  • In segmented-page mapping, a logical address is split into three fields: segment, page, and word. The segment number indexes a segment table, which points to the base of that segment’s own page table; the page number then indexes into that page table to obtain a block number, which combines with the word offset to give the physical address.
  • Because this scheme needs two extra memory accesses (segment table, then page table) before the real memory access, a fast associative memory is used to cache the most recently used (segment, page) → block translations. This is called a Translation Look-aside Buffer (TLB). On a TLB hit the mapping is available immediately; only on a TLB miss is the slower two-table walk performed.
Figure 12-21 — Mapping in a segmented-page memory management unit (Mano, p.478): (a) logical-to-physical address mapping via a segment table and page table; (b) the associative-memory TLB, indexed by segment and page, that shortcuts this walk.

3.3 Worked numerical example (Mano’s example, adapted)

WORKED EXAMPLE

A logical address specifies 16 possible segments, each of up to 256 pages of 256 words each (logical address = 4-bit segment + 8-bit page + 8-bit word = 20 bits). Physical memory is 220 words, divided into 4096 blocks of 256 words each (physical address = 12-bit block + 8-bit word).

Suppose logical address 6 / 02 / 7E (segment 6, page 2, offset 7E hex) is referenced. The segment table says segment 6’s page table starts at address 35; that page table’s entry for page 2 (at address 35+2=37) gives block number 019. So the physical address becomes block 019, offset 7E — and because segment 6/page 2 was just referenced, the pair (6,2)→019 is also written into the associative TLB, so the next reference to segment 6 page 2 skips the table walk entirely.

Figure 12-24 — Logical-to-physical memory mapping example, all numbers in hexadecimal (Mano, p.481): the segment table and page table together resolve logical address 6/02/7E to physical block 019; the TLB caches this and one other recently-used (segment,page) pair.

3.4 Memory protection

  • Because memory is shared and moved around dynamically, protection must accompany every access. Rather than protecting the physical address directly (awkward, since blocks move), protection bits are attached to each segment-table or page-table entry — i.e. in the logical-address space, which stays fixed for a program even as its physical location changes.
  • A segment descriptor typically carries: a base address field (pointing to the segment’s page-table base, or block base), a length field (checked against the page/offset to catch out-of-range accesses — a size violation), and a protection field.
Figure 12-25 — Format of a typical segment descriptor (Mano, p.482): base address, length, and protection fields together let the MMU both translate and validate every access.
  • Common protection levels an operating system assigns via the descriptor: full read/write (given to a program for its own instructions/data), read-only (for shared utility/library routines so many programs can read them but none can modify them), execute-only (a segment can be fetched as instructions but not read as data, protecting compiled code from being copied), and system-only (reserved for operating-system segments, inaccessible to ordinary user programs).

CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING

  1. List the three basic components/responsibilities of a memory management unit. [3M]
  2. What is a Translation Look-aside Buffer, and why is associative memory well suited to implementing it? [6M]
  3. Distinguish a logical address (in a segmented system) from a virtual address (in a pure paging system). [4M]
  4. Trace how a segmented-page MMU translates a logical address into a physical address when the TLB misses. [6M]
  5. What fields make up a segment descriptor, and what does each protect against? [4M]
  6. Why is protection information attached to the logical address (segment/page table) rather than to the physical address directly? [4M]
